trial_allocation.allocation_rationale: Baseline model — fixed defaults, no HPO needed.

Lasso has a small search space (primarily alpha). 4 trials are sufficient to explore a range of regularization strengths given the modest feature count (24) and large sample size (4604). More trials would yield diminishing returns.

Random forest has moderate complexity (n_estimators, max_depth, min_samples_split). With 4604 samples, 6 trials allow exploration of key parameters without excessive computational cost. It is less sensitive to hyperparameters than boosting.

Gradient boosting (sklearn) has moderate sensitivity to learning_rate, n_estimators, and max_depth. 6 trials provide a fair search given that it shares the boosting concept with xgboost but is often slower to converge.

XGBoost is the most promising model for low MAE on this dataset, but it has the largest and most sensitive hyperparameter set (n_estimators, learning_rate, max_depth, subsample, colsample_bytree, regularization). 8 trials are allocated to thoroughly explore its search space within the 30-trial budget.

SVR with RBF kernel requires tuning of C and gamma, but training time per trial is higher due to quadratic complexity. 6 trials balance the need to find good parameters with the risk of excessive runtime. Its expected performance is lower than boosting, so it receives fewer trials than xgboost.

decision_rationale.reason: XGBoost is a state‑of‑the‑art gradient boosting library, known for top performance on tabular benchmarks including materials property prediction. Given 4604 samples and 24 features, it can learn complex interactions.
evidence: XGBoost consistently wins Kaggle competitions on tabular data.
Matbench studies show XGBoost outperforming random forest and linear models for band gap prediction.
decision_rationale.fallback: If overfitting or training time too long, reduce number of trials or fallback to gradient_boosting.
decision_rationale.expected_performance: Expected to yield lowest MAE among all candidates if properly tuned.

evidence: SVR has been successfully applied to small‑to‑medium materials datasets.
Kernel trick allows flexibility without manual feature engineering.

model_strategy.model_selection_rationale_summary: Selected models cover a spectrum from interpretable linear regularization (ridge, lasso) to non‑linear tree ensembles (random forest, gradient boosting, xgboost) and support vector regression. XGBoost added as a high‑performance boosting method leveraging its state‑of‑the‑art results on materials data. Ridge serves as a fast, interpretable baseline. Deep learning is excluded due to limited dataset size and low interpretability. KNN is excluded for poor scalability and lack of mechanistic insight. Gaussian processes are omitted due to computational cost and limited advantage on medium‑sized data.
